title: Fungi, Lichens and Algae

toc.title: 3.1 Fungi: the four classes; yeast and Mucor
3.3 Algae: green, red and brown; Spirogyra

html:
This chapter of the Biodiversity unit carries about 2 of the 40 Botany questions. They come from three short lists: the four classes of fungi (their mycelium, spores and fruiting bodies, and which disease each causes); the partners and growth forms of lichens; and the three classes of algae told apart by pigment, stored food and flagella. On top of these, the paper expects the life histories of three type organisms — yeast, Mucor and Spirogyra — in enough detail to answer "which spore", "which stage is diploid" and "how many filaments come from one zygospore".

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Fungal classes by spore — Phycomycetes zygospore or oospore, Ascomycetes ascospores (endogenous, 8), Basidiomycetes basidiospores (exogenous, 4), Deuteromycetes no sexual spore.
  • Disease ↔ fungus — late blight of potato (Phytophthora), white rust of mustard (Albugo), rust of wheat (Puccinia), smut (Ustilago), ergot (Claviceps), red rot of sugarcane (Colletotrichum).
  • Yeast — budding, zymase, C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, ascus with 4 ascospores, haplo-diplontic cycle.
  • Mucor — coenocytic mycelium, sporangium with columella, heterothallic conjugation, zygospore as the only diploid stage.
  • Lichens — mycobiont + phycobiont; crustose, foliose, fruticose; soredia and isidia; pollution indicators and pioneers.
  • Algae — green (chl a, b; starch), brown (chl a, c, fucoxanthin; laminarin, mannitol; algin), red (chl a, phycoerythrin; floridean starch; agar; no flagella).
  • Spirogyra — spiral chloroplasts with pyrenoids, scalariform and lateral conjugation, zygotic meiosis, one filament per zygospore.

3.1 Fungi: the four classes; yeast and Mucor

General characters

Fungi are eukaryotic, achlorophyllous, heterotrophic thallophytes. They digest food outside the body and absorb it — as saprophytes (on dead matter), parasites (on living hosts) or symbionts (in lichens and mycorrhizae). The body is a mycelium, a mass of thread-like hyphae that are either aseptate and coenocytic (multinucleate, no cross walls) or septate. The wall is of chitin (fungal cellulose), and the reserve food is glycogen and oil — never starch. The study of fungi is mycology.

Sexual reproduction has three steps: plasmogamy (fusion of protoplasts), karyogamy (fusion of nuclei) and meiosis. In Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes karyogamy is delayed, so the hyphae pass through a dikaryotic (n + n) stage with two nuclei per cell.

Feature Phycomycetes (algal fungi) Ascomycetes (sac fungi) Basidiomycetes (club fungi) Deuteromycetes (fungi imperfecti)
Mycelium aseptate, coenocytic septate, branched (yeast unicellular) septate, with clamp connections; long dikaryotic phase septate, branched
Asexual spores endogenous sporangiospores (Mucor) or motile zoospores (Albugo, Phytophthora) exogenous conidia on conidiophores; budding in yeast rare (conidia, oidia); fragmentation common conidia only
Sexual spores zygospore (isogamous fusion of gametangia) or oospore (oogamy) ascospores, usually 8, formed endogenously in a sac, the ascus basidiospores, 4, formed exogenously on a club-shaped basidium; no sex organs — two vegetative hyphae fuse (somatogamy) not known
Fruiting body none ascocarp — cleistothecium (closed), perithecium (flask), apothecium (cup) basidiocarp — mushroom, bracket fungus, puffball none
Examples Mucor, Rhizopus, Albugo, Phytophthora, Pythium Saccharomyces, Penicillium, Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora, Morchella, Ophiocordyceps Agaricus, Pleurotus, Ganoderma, Puccinia, Ustilago, Amanita, Lycoperdon Alternaria, Colletotrichum, Trichoderma, Fusarium, Cercospora, Helminthosporium
Diseases late blight of potato (Phytophthora infestans — the Irish famine), white rust of crucifers (Albugo candida, on mustard and radish), damping-off (Pythium) ergot of rye (Claviceps purpurea), powdery mildew (Erysiphe) black stem rust of wheat (Puccinia graminis), loose smut of wheat (Ustilago) early blight of potato (Alternaria solani), red rot of sugarcane (Colletotrichum falcatum), tikka of groundnut (Cercospora), brown spot of rice (Helminthosporium), ringworm
The four classes by their sexual spore

Zygo-Asco-Basidio-None: PhycoZ, Asco = sac with 8 inside, Basidio = club with 4 outside, Deutero = none known. "Asco inside, Basidio outside" settles most spore questions.

Old names and moving targets
  • When the sexual stage of a deuteromycete is found, it is moved to Ascomycetes or Basidiomycetes; most fungi imperfecti turn out to be ascomycetes.
  • Phytophthora, Albugo and Pythium (Oomycetes) have cellulose walls and are no longer counted as true fungi, but the CEE syllabus still lists them under Phycomycetes — answer accordingly.
  • Yarsagumba (Ophiocordyceps sinensis) is an ascomycete that parasitises a caterpillar — see Chapter 5.

Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae)

Structure. Yeast is a unicellular ascomycete (no mycelium), with oval cells about 5–10 μm long. Each cell has a thin wall (glucans and mannans with a little chitin), a plasma membrane, a large central vacuole with volutin granules, one nucleus beside it, mitochondria, and reserve food as glycogen and oil droplets. It is a facultative anaerobe: with oxygen it respires completely; without oxygen it ferments sugar with the enzyme complex zymase (Buchner, 1897):

C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + energy (2 ATP per glucose)

Reproduction.

Method What happens
Budding (main vegetative method) a small outgrowth (bud) appears; the nucleus divides and one daughter nucleus enters the bud, which enlarges and breaks off, leaving a bud scar. In rich sugar medium buds stay attached in chains — a pseudomycelium
Fission the cell divides into two by a septum — in fission yeast, Schizosaccharomyces
Ascospore formation (sexual) two haploid cells of opposite mating type fuse (plasmogamy + karyogamy) → a diploid cell; it may bud as a diploid, and later turns into an ascus: meiosis gives 4 haploid ascospores, which are released and bud as haploid cells

Because both haploid and diploid cells of S. cerevisiae bud and grow, its life cycle is haplo-diplontic. (Schizosaccharomyces octosporus is haplontic, with 8 ascospores; Saccharomycodes ludwigii is diplontic.)

Uses. Baking (CO₂ raises the dough), brewing of beer and wine, and in Nepal the murcha (marcha) starter used for jaand and raksi, in which moulds such as Mucor and Rhizopus break starch into sugar and yeasts ferment it; vitamin B complex and single-cell protein; recombinant hepatitis B vaccine; and the model eukaryote of genetics (first eukaryotic genome sequenced, 1996). Candida albicans, a yeast-like fungus, causes candidiasis.

Mucor (pin mould)

Structure. Mucor (Phycomycetes, class Zygomycetes in newer books) grows as a white cottony mycelium on moist bread, cow dung, rotting fruit and vegetables. The hyphae are branched, aseptate and coenocytic (septa form only to cut off reproductive organs), with chitin walls and glycogen and oil as food. Unlike Rhizopus, Mucor has no rhizoids and no stolons; its sporangiophores arise singly from the mycelium.

Asexual reproduction. Erect, aerial sporangiophores each end in a round, black sporangium. Its central sterile dome is the columella; around it are many non-motile sporangiospores (aplanospores). The sporangial wall dissolves or breaks, the spores are blown away and each germinates into a new mycelium. In poor conditions Mucor also forms thick-walled, intercalary chlamydospores; in sugary liquid it buds into yeast-like oidia.

Sexual reproduction (conjugation). Most species are heterothallic — zygospores form only when hyphae of two compatible strains, + and −, meet (Blakeslee, 1904, discovered heterothallism in Mucor mucedo). The steps:

  1. Short side branches of + and − hyphae grow towards each other and touch — progametangia.
  2. Each tip is cut off by a septum as a multinucleate gametangium; the stalk behind it is the suspensor.
  3. The wall between the two gametangia dissolves and their contents fuse (plasmogamy); + and − nuclei pair and fuse (karyogamy).
  4. The fused cell becomes a thick, black, warty-walled resting zygospore (2n) — the only diploid stage.
  5. On germination, meiosis occurs and the zygospore puts out a germ sporangium (promycelium + sporangium) whose spores give + and − mycelia.

A zygospore that forms without fusion is an azygospore (parthenospore). Since the only diploid structure is the zygote, the life cycle is haplontic with zygotic meiosis.

Feature Mucor Rhizopus Yeast
Class Phycomycetes Phycomycetes Ascomycetes
Body coenocytic mycelium coenocytic mycelium with rhizoids and stolons single cells
Asexual sporangiospores; chlamydospores; oidia sporangiospores (sporangiophores in tufts over rhizoids) budding, fission
Sexual spore zygospore zygospore ascospores (4) in an ascus
Diploid stage zygospore only zygospore only zygote, and diploid budding cells

3.2 Lichens: introduction and types

A lichen is a composite organism: a stable, self-supporting symbiotic association between a fungus (the mycobiont) and an alga or a cyanobacterium (the phycobiont or photobiont). The fungus forms most of the body, absorbs water and minerals and shelters the alga; the alga photosynthesises and feeds both. (Because the fungus gains more and can penetrate the algal cells, some authors call it controlled parasitism, or helotism.) The mycobiont is usually an ascomycete; the phycobiont is usually a green alga (Trebouxia, Trentepohlia) or a cyanobacterium (Nostoc). Lichenology is the study of lichens.

Basis Types Examples
Growth form crustose — a thin crust tightly glued to rock or bark, cannot be removed whole Graphis, Lecanora, Rhizocarpon
foliose — flat, lobed, leaf-like; attached loosely by rhizines Parmelia, Peltigera, Physcia
fruticose — shrubby, branched, erect or hanging; attached by a basal disc Usnea (old man's beard), Cladonia (reindeer moss), Ramalina
Internal structure homoiomerous — algal cells scattered evenly among hyphae Collema, Leptogium
heteromerous — algal cells in a distinct layer: upper cortex, algal zone, medulla, lower cortex Parmelia, Physcia, Usnea
Fungal partner ascolichens (most), basidiolichens, deuterolichens Parmelia; Cora

Reproduction. Vegetatively by fragmentation, by soredia (tiny granules of a few algal cells wrapped in hyphae, dispersed by wind) and by isidia (coral-like outgrowths of the thallus that break off); the fungus alone reproduces sexually, forming apothecia or perithecia, and its spores must find a suitable alga to form a new lichen.

Importance. - Pioneers: crustose lichens are the first colonisers of bare rock in a xerosere; their acids (oxalic acid, lichen acids) weather the rock and start soil formation. - Air-pollution indicators: they are very sensitive to SO₂, so they disappear from polluted city air. - Food and trade: reindeer moss (Cladonia rangiferina) feeds reindeer; in Nepal, lichens (jhyau, mostly of the family Parmeliaceae) are collected in the hills and exported to India for spice mixes, dyes and perfume resins. - Dyes and chemicals: litmus (from Roccella), orchil dye; oak moss (Evernia) in perfumes; usnic acid of Usnea is antibacterial.

3.3 Algae: green, red and brown; Spirogyra

General characters

Algae are simple, chlorophyll-bearing, thalloid, autotrophic and mostly aquatic eukaryotes. They have no roots, stems, leaves or vascular tissue; their sex organs are usually unicellular and not covered by a jacket of sterile cells, and the zygote does not grow into an embryo. They range from unicellular (Chlamydomonas, Chlorella) and colonial (Volvox) to filamentous (Spirogyra, Ulothrix) and large parenchymatous thalli (Ulva, Laminaria). Sexual reproduction is isogamous (gametes alike), anisogamous (unlike in size) or oogamous (a large non-motile egg and a small motile sperm — Volvox, Fucus). Their study is phycology.

Feature Chlorophyceae (green algae) Phaeophyceae (brown algae) Rhodophyceae (red algae)
Main pigments chlorophyll a, b, carotenoids chlorophyll a, c, fucoxanthin chlorophyll a (d in some), r-phycoerythrin, phycocyanin
Stored food starch (around pyrenoids) laminarin and mannitol floridean starch
Cell wall cellulose cellulose + algin (alginic acid) cellulose, pectin and sulphated polysaccharides (agar, carrageenan)
Flagella 2–8, equal, apical 2, unequal, lateral none — no motile cells
Habitat fresh water, brackish and sea water, moist soil mostly marine, cool seas mostly marine, often in deep water
Body unicellular to parenchymatous filaments to giant kelps with holdfast, stipe and frond; air bladders filaments to complex thalli
Sexual reproduction iso-, aniso- or oogamous iso-, aniso- or oogamous oogamous, with complex post-fertilisation stages
Examples Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra, Chara, Ulva, Chlorella Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Fucus, Sargassum Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gelidium, Gracilaria, Batrachospermum (fresh water)
Pigment and food in one line

Green — a, b, starch. Brown — a, c, fucoxanthin; laminarin, mannitol; algin. Red — a, phycoerythrin; floridean starch; agar; no flagella. Red algae live deepest because phycoerythrin absorbs the blue-green light that penetrates furthest into the sea.

Products to remember: agar (Gelidium, Gracilaria) for culture media and jellies; carrageenan (Chondrus) and algin (Laminaria, Macrocystis) as thickeners; Porphyra (nori) and Laminaria (kombu) as food; Chlorella and Spirulina (a cyanobacterium) as protein supplements; kelps as a source of iodine and potash.

Spirogyra — structure

Spirogyra ("water silk", "pond scum") is a free-floating, unbranched, filamentous green alga of still fresh water — ponds, ditches and paddy fields. Its slimy feel comes from a mucilage sheath of pectin outside the cellulose wall. All cells of the filament are alike and each can divide: there is no division of labour.

Each cylindrical cell has: - a two-layered wall (inner cellulose, outer pectin); - a thin lining layer of cytoplasm and a large central vacuole; - a single nucleus suspended in the centre of the vacuole by cytoplasmic strands; - one to several ribbon-shaped, spirally coiled chloroplasts with smooth or wavy margins, each carrying a row of pyrenoids (centres of starch formation).

The filament is haploid (n).

Spirogyra — reproduction

  • Vegetative: fragmentation — the filament breaks and each piece grows by cell division. This is the commonest method.
  • Asexual (rare): akinetes (thick-walled vegetative cells), aplanospores, and azygospores (parthenospores — formed from a gamete that fails to fuse).
  • Sexual: by conjugation. The gametes are non-flagellate and amoeboid (aplanogametes). They look alike (morphologically isogamous), but one — called male, the + strain — moves into the other, which stays put: the process is physiologically anisogamous.
Scalariform conjugation Lateral conjugation
Between cells of two filaments lying side by side adjacent cells of the same filament
Thallus heterothallic homothallic
How papillae from opposite cells meet and form conjugation tubes, giving a ladder-like look; the contents of each male cell round off and pass through the tube indirect (chain-forming): a tube forms beside the septum between neighbouring cells; direct: the gamete passes through a pore in the septum
After it one filament empty (male), the other with a zygospore in each cell (female) alternate cells empty and alternate cells with zygospores

The zygospore and meiosis. The zygote secretes a thick three-layered wall (exospore, mesospore, endospore) and becomes a resting zygospore (2n) that survives drought and cold. On germination its diploid nucleus divides by meiosis into four haploid nuclei; three degenerate and one survives, so each zygospore gives only one new filament. Meiosis is zygotic and the life cycle is haplontic — the zygospore is the only diploid cell.

Count the filaments correctly

One zygospore of Spirogyra → meiosis → 4 haploid nuclei → 3 degenerate → 1 new filament. Options of "4 filaments" (forgetting the degeneration) or "2 filaments" are the standard distractors. In Mucor, by contrast, one zygospore gives a germ sporangium with many spores.

Chapter summary

  • Fungi are eukaryotic, achlorophyllous absorptive heterotrophs with chitin walls and glycogen and oil as food; their sexual cycle is plasmogamy, karyogamy, meiosis.
  • Phycomycetes have coenocytic hyphae and zygospores or oospores; Ascomycetes form 8 endogenous ascospores in an ascus; Basidiomycetes form 4 exogenous basidiospores on a basidium; Deuteromycetes have no known sexual stage.
  • Phytophthora (late blight), Albugo (white rust), Claviceps (ergot), Puccinia (rust), Ustilago (smut), Alternaria (early blight) and Colletotrichum (red rot) are the classic disease fungi.
  • Yeast is a unicellular ascomycete that buds, ferments sugar with zymase to ethanol and CO₂, and forms 4 ascospores; its cycle is haplo-diplontic.
  • Mucor has a coenocytic mycelium without rhizoids, sporangia with a columella, heterothallic conjugation and a zygospore that is its only diploid stage.
  • A lichen is a fungus (mycobiont) living with an alga or cyanobacterium (phycobiont); its forms are crustose, foliose and fruticose, and it spreads by soredia and isidia.
  • Lichens are pioneers on bare rock and sensitive indicators of SO₂ pollution.
  • Green algae store starch and have chl a, b; brown algae store laminarin and mannitol and have fucoxanthin and algin; red algae store floridean starch, have phycoerythrin and agar, and never have flagella.
  • Spirogyra is a haploid unbranched filament with spiral chloroplasts; it reproduces by fragmentation and by scalariform or lateral conjugation; one zygospore gives one filament after zygotic meiosis.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (c) — Fungi store glycogen and oil; starch is the store of plants and green algae, floridean starch of red algae.

2. (a) — Phycomycetes (Mucor, Rhizopus, Albugo) have aseptate, multinucleate hyphae; the other three classes have septate hyphae.

3. (d) — Ascospores form inside the ascus after meiosis (usually followed by one mitosis, giving 8). Exogenous spores on sterigmata are basidiospores.

4. (b) — "Imperfect" means the perfect (sexual) stage is unknown; they reproduce only by conidia.

5. (b) — The mushroom is a basidiocarp bearing gills lined with basidia. Ascocarps and cleistothecia belong to Ascomycetes.

6. (d) — Late blight of potato is caused by Phytophthora infestans (an oomycete, listed under Phycomycetes). Rust and smut are basidiomycetes; red rot is a deuteromycete.

7. (a) — Budding is the usual method; fission occurs only in fission yeasts, and yeast has no zoospores.

8. (c) — Zymase (Buchner, 1897) converts glucose to ethanol and CO₂. Invertase splits sucrose; diastase splits starch.

9. (d) — The columella is the sterile dome inside the sporangium. The apophysis is the swelling below the sporangium in Rhizopus; the suspensor supports a gametangium.

10. (c) — Mucor forms a zygospore by fusion of two gametangia. Oospores belong to oogamous Phycomycetes such as Albugo.

11. (b) — The mycobiont is the fungus; the phycobiont (photobiont) is the alga or cyanobacterium.

12. (a) — Usnea is a shrubby, hanging fruticose lichen; its internal structure is heteromerous, so (d) is wrong.

13. (c) — Lichens absorb everything from rain and air and cannot excrete it; SO₂ destroys their chlorophyll, so they vanish from polluted towns.

14. (d) — Soredia contain both partners and are blown away. Isidia are outgrowths of the thallus; rhizines attach a foliose lichen.

15. (a) — Green algae have the same pigments as land plants: chlorophyll a and b. Option (b) is brown algae, (c) red algae, (d) cyanobacteria.

16. (b) — Brown algae store laminarin (a polysaccharide) and mannitol (a sugar alcohol).

17. (a) — Agar comes from the red algae Gelidium and Gracilaria. Laminaria and Fucus are brown algae that yield algin.

18. (c) — Red algae have no flagellated stage at all; even their male gametes (spermatia) are non-motile. They do have chlorophyll a, walls and oogamous sex.

19. (b) — One or more ribbon-shaped chloroplasts coil spirally round each cell. Cup-shaped is Chlamydomonas; girdle-shaped is Ulothrix.

20. (d) — Meiosis gives four haploid nuclei, three degenerate, and the one survivor grows into one filament.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (b) — Rhizopus has root-like rhizoids and creeping stolons, with sporangiophores in tufts; Mucor has neither. Both have a columella, coenocytic hyphae and zygospores.

2. (d) — Only the zygospore is 2n; meiosis happens when it germinates, so the mycelium, spores and gametangia are all haploid.

3. (a) — Heterothallism (Blakeslee, 1904): fusion needs + and − strains. Homothallic species form zygospores within one mycelium.

4. (c) — Fermentation of sugar by zymase gives CO₂ bubbles that are trapped in the dough. The ethanol evaporates during baking.

5. (c) — Basidia bear four basidiospores outside, on sterigmata. Ascomycetes form spores inside asci; both have septate hyphae and both form fruiting bodies.

6. (a) — Classification by sexual stage: once asci are found, the fungus is an ascomycete. Conidia, septa and antibiotics occur in deuteromycetes too.

7. (d) — The phycobiont is the only partner with chlorophyll; the mycobiont forms the body, holds water and absorbs minerals. Only cyanobacterial partners fix nitrogen.

8. (b) — Lichen acids slowly corrode rock and dead lichen adds organic matter, starting the soil that mosses need next. Lichens have no roots.

9. (a) — Red and violet light are absorbed near the surface; the blue-green light that penetrates deepest is absorbed by phycoerythrin. Red algae lack chlorophyll b.

10. (d) — The two gametes are identical in form (isogamous) but behave differently: one is active (male, + strain), the other passive. Spirogyra gametes have no flagella.

11. (b) — All male cells empty into the female filament, which then holds a zygospore in each cell. Option (c) describes lateral conjugation.

12. (c) — Zygotic meiosis means the zygote divides by meiosis; every other cell in the cycle is haploid.

1. (d) — Meiosis of the 2n nucleus gives 4 haploid nuclei; three degenerate and one survives to form a single filament.

2. (b) — Four exogenous spores on a basidium and no sex organs mark a basidiomycete — wheat rust (Puccinia) or smut (Ustilago).

3. (a) — Asci and ascospores are the sexual stage of Ascomycetes; once it is known the fungus leaves the "imperfect" group.

4. (c) — 18 g ÷ 180 g mol⁻¹ = 0.1 mol glucose → 0.2 mol CO₂ × 44 g mol⁻¹ = 8.8 g. Option (b), 9.2 g, is the ethanol (0.2 × 46).

6. (d) — Holdfast–stipe–frond, laminarin and mannitol, and two unequal lateral flagella are the marks of brown algae (Laminaria).
